newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU/US seem keen to avoid Boeing at summit.
newsitem.headline: EU/US seem keen to avoid Boeing at summit.

text.p: The United States and the European Union appear keen to avoid bringing up one of the most contentious issues facing them when they hold a summit in the Hague on Wednesday -- the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger.
Both sides have said in briefings leading up to the twice-yearly summit that they have no plans to discuss the $14 billion merger.

Although the European Commission, the EU's antitrust watchdog, has expressed grave concerns about the effect on competition of the deal, the official line is that nothing can be discussed because nothing has been decided.
"We have no particular wish to raise the issue of Boeing. The issue is still under investigation," the Commission's chief spokesman, Nikolaus van der Pas said on Monday.
It echoed the comments of U.S. officials last week.
"The president will be hard put to comment because we are still looking at it," one U.S. official said.
As well as the Commission, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission is also investigating the deal under which aerospace giant Boeing would take over defence contractor McDonnell Douglas .
The FTC has barely made any comment about the deal or its investigation. The Commission, by contrast, has been vociferous about its problems.
In a statement of objections sent last week, the Commission noted that the deal would leave the world market with only two major commercial aircraft manufacturers -- Boeing and Airbus Industrie.
Airbus is a consortium of France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace, Germany's DASA and Spain's Construcciones Aeronautiocas.

The merger would increase Boeing's share of the market for large aircraft -- with a capacity of more than 100 seats -- to 70 percent, given McDonnell's six percent share of total aircraft orders at the end of 1996.
The Commission, however, is said to be most concerned by Boeing's long-term exclusive supply deals with American Airlines and Delta Air Lines .
Across the Atlantic, U.S. senators have begun lobbying Clinton to make sure the U.S. firms get a fair deal from the Europeans.
For that reason alone, both sides are expected to arrive at the summit prepared to discuss the issue, even if neither plans to bring it up.
